We saw in the minutes of the government sessions that they discussed giving loans to Crisis Staffs. We'll see in Trnovo a similar assistance given from the government. Given that I read this phrase, "pomoc SRBiH" it makes more sense to read it's aid from the government. If it's "aid to," it could perhaps be voluntary subscriptions from people, people just voluntary sending money and aid to the government. But it's 5 million dinars, I don't know -- there's not enough indication here to say it came from the government, but we've seen that elsewhere. As to how the resources were allocated, we simply see in the government minutes that they discussed requests from different Crisis Staffs, but no indication in the minutes of various merits of these Crisis Staffs. Also, other sources of income, according to this - could you put the translation back up - money from a petrol station, money from a cafe, and municipal accounts from the Giro account, it says, so preexisting Municipal accounts. We'll see also in Trnovo other sources of municipal income.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But my question was the following: There was no regulation stating that each Crisis Staff would receive a specific budget. Because when we look at this, everything seems to be a bit anarchic, money cashed by a park bar, withdrawn from a Giro account, from a petrol station. Do you have any comments about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as we saw, the Crisis Staffs take over all the competencies and duties of the municipal assembly, and municipal governments were financed from various local taxes as well as from -- I'm talking about the preexisting system. The municipality would have its own accounts, would have local taxes and then aid from the state. I'm not an expert -- I'm not that familiar with the previous financial systems. But when the Crisis Staffs took over the municipal government, they also took over the municipal accounts. So we see that the bulk of their money coming from the municipal accounts. There is nothing in the documents, the normative documents we've seen, that set out how Crisis Staffs should operate. There's no mention of their budget. So I can't tell you more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, let me ask you a couple more questions to follow up on the Judge's question. With regard to this, you've described the 5 million dinar amount as aid from the republic. And it seems to make sense that it is from rather than to, because this is in the column listing their assets as opposed to --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I think that's a more logical interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And a question about the preexisting system of collecting taxes, are you familiar with the acronym SDK?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the social accounting office. It's called -- every municipality would have this -- it was an important -- one of the important municipal organs. Payments were made as the way of transferring payments between companies and governments and bodies and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that was in existence before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But taking one of the -- a common pattern we see in takeovers includes taking over the SDK offices and therefore getting control of their assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was something that was discussed in the planning stages?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We see Karadzic makes reference to it in an October speech as one of the things that they should -- institutions which the Serbs must control -- get control of, he says, even in those municipalities where we maybe have the majority, we still haven't gotten control of all our institutions, including the SDK.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to the Judge's questions about who made decisions about which Crisis Staffs might receive which amounts of money from the republic, have you seen anything in the documentation, other than something like we discussed yesterday, I believe, in government minutes where they were -- had an agenda item talking about loans to Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beyond those government -- we see -- I know we see some specific discussion of that in Trnovo. But at a larger level, on a larger -- a discussion at the republican level of how to allocate funds, I'm not familiar with anything at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, this sort of concludes our discussion about the support of the military by Crisis Staffs, and I think we're ready to move on and talk about relations between the Crisis Staffs and the police. Was there anything else you wanted to say in summing up on military and Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd just like to say that the military question is the most complicated, with the most variables, so it's been a little, perhaps, hard to sort out. The bottom line, the common denominator everywhere, is the coordination and the support, the commonality of purpose. As Subotic says, they were minor disagreements, but they were minor, and it was over who actually may be ordering. But the consistent pattern we see on that question everywhere is close coordination and support. Similarly for police -- not similarly. For police, it is a simpler picture, not so many variables. So we see many orders to police, and we'll get to that section now. I'm saying we're putting the hard part behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. To segue into that, we're going to show some documents regarding the police relations with Crisis Staffs. You say the picture was simpler or more consistent in what way with the police?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As stipulated in the 19 December instructions in municipal Crisis Staffs -- municipal Crisis Staffs, we do so the head of the police, either the chief of the police station or the commander of the police, as members of the Crisis Staff. We see reports from police to the Crisis Staffs on their operations in the municipalities. We see orders from the Crisis Staffs to the police. That is, again, consistent with how the police functioned. They had their own command structure, of course, but taskings would be given at the municipal level. They didn't get their day-to-day taskings from their ministry. We also see Crisis Staffs involved in setting up the police forces, setting up Serbian police forces, taking over police stations and dismissing non-Serbs from the police. Again, this is consistent with the 19 December instructions, which, for both variant A and B, stipulate mobilising Serbs into the reserve police forces and taking over the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me turn, then, to presentation tab 181, master tab 74. I think you have a couple of examples for us of the creation of separate Serb police departments within the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A few examples. This is -- the first one is from Brcko. This is a summary of the events and situations, basically a summary -- from internal evidence of -- yeah, it's signed the War Presidency at the last page, it's signed the War Presidency of Brcko municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that a summary of the activity --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the War Presidency, or the events in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you direct us to the excerpt you want to --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's on page 3 in the English translation. I'm -- it's on page 4 in the B/C/S, that is, 00741400. It's the fourth paragraph in the B/C/S, and the third paragraph in the English page 3. "When the war began, various military formations started to arrive in Brcko to help out. Since Brcko was part --" No, I'm sorry, I'm reading the wrong -- forgive me, I'm reading the -- I was reading the wrong one. "When the war began and the public security station was taken over, the same day, the War Presidency appointed Dragan Veselic chief of the public security station and began staffing the station with new people, including Serbs who had been employed there before." So a description of the War Presidency's role in setting up a Serb police -- police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you tab 182 in the presentation, master tab 285, from another municipality. Actually, this document appears to be a Ministry of Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia, concerning statements of policemen who had worked before the war broke out and were removed.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see from the date, the 24th of March, 1992. It's at the very -- it's from very early on. So I think their statements are of interest. And the policemen's account of what happened, it's on -- in the original, 02048151, the second paragraph; similarly on page 2 of the translation, the second paragraph. These policemen report that they've met with the chief of the public security station in Pale, when they went to -- where they worked, and the chief of police, Malko Koroman "informed them of the decision by the Crisis Staff of Pale municipality and the government of the Romanija Serb Autonomous District, that all policemen of Muslim nationality must hand in their weapons and equipment issued to them." So some policemen are recounting in this statement their experience that they were told the Crisis Staff had decided that they could no longer work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, after separate Serb police stations or commands were formed in the municipalities, did you see examples that they were working closely with the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw many examples of orders from the Crisis Staff to the municipal -- the police in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you tab 183 in the presentation, master tab 278. This is from Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a "Summary of conclusions, orders, and decisions adopted by the Crisis Staff/War Presidency relating to the SJB and the regional command from the 29th of May to the 24th of July, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you want to highlight some of those particular decisions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of those decisions. On the second page, number 2, "The order to military police and SJB organs to confiscate all illegally confiscated or misappropriated property." This order requires the police to immediately report to the Crisis Staff on their execution of this order. Further down on that same page: "The order of the 6th of June, 1992, obliging the SJB to use its members to control not just the Pecani settlement but also the other parts of town, and not to allow people to arbitrarily stay at or move into the homes of relatives and friends." On the third page of the translation, in the middle of the page, "The order of the 17th of June, requiring the SJB and regional command to form within two days a unified intervention platoon with 20 members each, with a basic task of preventing theft and other criminal activities." And the last one we'll look at again in a slightly different context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis. If this is a suitable moment for you to have the break, then we'll have the break until 10 minutes to 1.00, and then continue for another 55 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I think we're still talking about Crisis Staffs and dealing with the local police. I want to go to tab 184 in the presentation, master tab 289. This is another document from Prijedor. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I, before we start this, is it possible for me to ask for some clarification from the Chamber? Your Honour asked me to look into that document from the logistics base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I'm just wondering, I understand my -- that I cannot talk about my testimony with any of my colleagues, but may I inquire of them if they have had occasion to learn more about that document, or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I invited the witness to see whether she could find any further source. If she would limit her communications with her colleagues just to any information that might be found, and to whom it was addressed or whom would have received --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or other copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or other copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that seems very practical, and we'd have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you're allowed to do so, but limited to that subject.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, that document, master tab 289, presentation 184. Another document from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a document from the chief of the public security station, Simo Drljaca, to the Crisis Staff of Prijedor, dated the 1st of June, 1992. It's in reference -- it's a report on the police implementation of orders of the Crisis Staff, so we're saying -- the police are saying the conclusion -- various conclusions, to what extent they are being observed and implemented. I would note here is reference, the first reference to conclusion number 02-111-108/92, "by which the release of prisoners is prohibited is being fully observed." We'll see that conclusion again in a moment. This is an indication of the reporting of the police to the Crisis Staff on the implementation of Crisis Staff orders and conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A couple more examples I want to show you that relate to police and Crisis Staff relations. Presentation tab 185, master tab 290, from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The conclusions of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most of the 27th of April, 1992. Under item 4, the Crisis Staff decides that Mirko Vrucinic conduct affairs of the head of the public safety station of Serbian municipality of Sanski Most. The Crisis Staff also proposes to the Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most to appoint Mladen Lukic as the president -- that's the executive committee, that's not relevant to the police, I'm sorry. Just the first sentence is relevant to the police. You will note -- we would note from earlier -- the earlier document on the composition of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff, that Mirko Vrucinic was a member of the Crisis Staff and they're appointing him as head of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And next, presentation tab 186, master tab 291, from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's an order of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most to the police station, the public security station, dated the 6th of June, ordering the police to evacuate 150 prisoners to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, that takes me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That takes me to another topic. Was there anything else you wanted to say about the interaction with the police before I go on to talk about Crisis Staffs and detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've only shown a few documents here, but in my report I also point the way to many other such documents on police. It's not a long section because I think it's fairly clear what the picture was, but I'd be glad to answer further questions about it, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. For now, then, let me turn to the issue of detention facilities. Were the Crisis Staffs involved in either the establishing or control or access to detention centres?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We see that in the municipalities, that Crisis Staffs, in some cases, set up detention centres, could order the detention or release of prisoners or the movement of prisoners. So we'll look at several documents that indicate the relationship between Crisis Staffs and detention centres in their municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that regard, then, let me show you presentation tab 187, master tab 295. First of all, tell us what this document is, and then direct us to the excerpted portions you wish to talk about.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a fairly lengthy document that I will refer to a number of times. I think we have them as separate tabs, just to not keep flipping back to this one. But it is a report compiled by the Banja Luka SCB, security services centre, on the basis of reports from the police of Prijedor, Bosanski Novi and Sanski Most. It says that this report was compiled pursuant to a decision of the chief of the security services centre of August 1992, and the report is dated August 1992. So the first part of the document we'll be looking at is a compilation of the different individual, three reports from those police. But it gives a good indication of what the police had to say about the events in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to two particular municipalities, can you tell us, is there an excerpt on page 1 regarding Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's an excerpt on the first page of the English text, which is apparently page 2 of the translation; in the B/C/S, it is -- the sentence begins on B0032527, but the bulk of the quote is the next page, B0032528. Referring to Prijedor, on the -- page 2 in the English translation, the middle paragraph: "The Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor decided to organise reception and accommodation in the settlement of Trnopolje for persons who sought protection, and that prisoners of war should be held for processing in the building of the Keraterm RO in Prijedor or in the administration building and workshop of the iron ore mine in Omarska."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at page 6 of the English, and I believe it's page 8, or B0032534, can you tell us what it says about detention facilities in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On page 6, at the beginning of the section on -- I'm sorry, it's -- it's the sixth page of the translation, but it's page 7 in my numbering here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My mistake.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of the section on Sanski Most. "From the beginning of the armed conflicts in the area of the municipality of Sanski Most, the end of May 1992, the municipal Crisis Staff made a decision ordering the setting up of collection and investigation centres in the premises of the sports hall, the facilities of Betonirka, and the large workshop of the Krings factory. As a result of a special decision of the Crisis Staff, a prison was set up in the Betonirka facility, a warden and assistant warden were appointed, and police employees were engaged in security matters together with members of the army." The next paragraph, one sentence in the middle of the next paragraph: "A number of persons were brought on the direct order of the municipality's Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take you to the next tab, which is 188 in the presentation, master tab 299. This relates to the role of a Crisis Staff and the establishment of a detention facility in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a report of the Prijedor police station, dated the 31st of May, 1992, sent to the Crisis Staff, among others, and also to police members. It's describing the establishment of the Omarska camp, noting that, in the first sentence, he says, "in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff," the police chief orders -- pardon me, "that the industrial compound of the Omarska strip mine shall serve as a provisional collection centre for people captured in combat or detained on the grounds of the security services operational information." It's a lengthy order describing all the steps of establishing the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that document was from whom?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the chief of the public security service, Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To whom was it addressed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you can tell.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's sent -- I was looking at the addressees at the end. There's no immediate addressee on the first page, but it is sent to the Crisis Staff, to the security services coordinator, to the security services in Banja Luka, to the chief of police, to the chief of security, to the director of the iron ore mines, and to files. And the indication on the -- there's some handwritten indications that would seem to say this copy was received by the iron ore mines and security, it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, tab 189 in the presentation, master tab 298. This is a document dated 8 July 1992, from Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the minutes of the War Presidency of Kotor Varos of 8 July 1992. Under item 1: "Due to problems in the work of the public security station, a decision has been made to use the hall in Piljana saw mill temporarily as a prison, and it's been recommended that all detained persons be transferred to the Piljana hall in the future."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Presentation tab 190, master tab 420. This is a document from the 20th of May, 1992, in Foca.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's from the warden of the penal and correction facility, Foca, dated the 20th of May, 1992, to the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Foca. "Request to appoint authorised persons. We hereby request the appointment of authorised persons for questioning and examination of captured persons who have been brought to the penal and correctional facility, Foca."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the name of the warden?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, presentation tab 191, which is master tab 301. This is from the 15th of May, 1992, from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A decision of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac, dated the 15th of May, 1992. "All people of Croatian nationality on the territory of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac shall be isolated and deployed to vital facilities in the town and in villages." Deployed, I would note the original is "rasporedjeni" sent to, or put in. Deployed sounds a bit military in this context. It's not wrong but ... I would also point out, in this context, according to the census of 1991, in Bosanski Samac, there were about 14.000 Croats, about 45 per cent of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I guess I didn't make the transitional point I wanted to make before when we were talking about Crisis Staff involvements in detention facilities. Now we're going to talk about particular people that are chosen to be placed in those facilities?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is obviously still dealing with detention facilities, but to show in addition to setting up detention centres, Crisis Staffs were ordering whole categories of people be detained. So although this is not specified which detention centre, I find it significant here, just the order of the Crisis Staff, that an entire category of people - in this case, Croatian nationality - be detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In a similar vein --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Terribly sorry to interrupt you. You've added one point, madam. You've said in that municipality, the municipality of Bosanski Samac, there were 14.000 Croats. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's based on the census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to find out, what was the total of the population proportionately speaking? What was the total amount of the population? Who were the other members of this municipality? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will bring next time the census -- the official census results. It was 45 per cent of the population. I do not recall right now what that means in total, but that would mean about 30.000 in total. It's 45 per cent were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judge what other ethnicities lived in Bosanski Samac, the significant numbers?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs were the other large number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a question in relation to this document to you as well. You said, or introductory said, it was those people selected as being sent to those prison facilities. If I read --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Detention is not -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I read the heading of this letter, then it says something about incessant bombardments, reasonable grounds that aircraft are being guided, that there's a collaboration with criminals, and that on the basis of that, all people of Croatian nationality on the territory shall be isolated and sent to, as you said it to us, to vital facilities in the town and in villages. I mean, I can't imagine that someone would understand this to be rather sending people not to detention facilities but to places where the municipal Crisis Staff would expect further bombardments to take place, and that it was not, therefore, mainly to detain them but rather to -- well, one might think of human shields as a measure of protection against bombardments. But since this document was introduced as a -- well, as the involvement of the municipal Crisis Staff with detention, I wonder, what makes you take this position and why you, as an expert, would say that the other interpretation would be the wrong one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not relating to one detention centre per se, and I think your interpretation of putting them in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said that one could possibly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree. One could, and I think that is a reasonable interpretation. But I would say that if you are identifying a category of all Croats and putting all of them in vital facilities as human shields, that seems to me is a form of detention. They're not -- it's not for their protection, it's not of their own free will, it's moving them, because they're Croats, to different places and keeping them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the other hand, if I can ask you a different question. You're talking about 14.000. At the same time -- therefore, I said it's a possible interpretation, because I would say managing 14.000 people as human shields is -- would not be an easy task. So therefore I'm also giving some opposite, but I'd rather first the expert answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave that figure to give you an idea of the makeup of Samac and how many people -- I have seen no other evidence that this -- that 14.000 people were rounded up and used as human shields. It does seem unlikely or impractical, given the numbers involved and that they were not -- the Serbs were not in overwhelming majority in that municipality to be able to control so many people. I see -- I think its intent is what's of interest here to me more than, perhaps, what -- whether this was -- whether that many people were actually detained, but that it was a category that the Crisis Staff thought it had the order -- the authority to decide the fate of those people in that way, to decide where they would be -- that they would be rounded up and sent somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Stewart, you were on your feet. Mr. Hannis was on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As Winston Churchill said of his understanding of mathematics, the moment has passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The moment has passed. You're sitting again. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A couple things, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In relation to the population figure, what was the date where that number comes from?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the 1991 census. As of May 1992, I know you're not an expert on Bosanski Samac, but was there any evidence that some of the Croatians may have left the municipality by that date?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no evidence from the census, since that was taken in 1991. In my general understanding of the conflict, yes, many Croats had left by then. But I couldn't point you to one piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know, but maybe it would be helpful to me if you could go to the original B/C/S where this statement about "All people of Croatian nationality" shall be put in isolation and taken to vital facilities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I do understand that the French translation was a bit behind. I think we're there again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies. Let me start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you read from the original B/C/S that sentence about "All people of Croatian nationality shall be put in isolation..." I want to hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With this decision, on the basis of this decision, in the territory of the municipality of -- Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac, all members of the Croatian ethnicity shall be taken into isolation and put up, distributed, in vital institutions in the town and the villages."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand the reading you had is one possible interpretation. I wasn't sure if it meant "put them in isolation and put them in vital facilities," or do some of each with parts. I think that's all I had on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to the next tab, unless there are further questions. If not, I'll go to presentation tab 192, master tab 302.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is minutes of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Petrovac - I would note that this time it's calling itself simply Petrovac - the 30th of June, 1992. On page 2 in the translation, under "Conclusions," this is on the bottom of the first page in the B/C/S: "Until the prison in Kozolua [phoen] is made operational, a plan should be made to arrest and bring in under custody all Muslims fit for military service who are thought to be capable of causing any harm to the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any information on the 1991 census population in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Petrovac was approximately - I'm sorry, I don't have it off the top - about 80 per cent Serb, and I'm -- in the order of magnitude, about 1.000 Muslims. I don't want to speak off the top of my head on that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think you indicated in your report, or perhaps somewhere else, that there were approximately 3.200 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3.200, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that now it was referring to itself simply as Petrovac as opposed to Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any significance to that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rejecting the Bosnian identification of Bosanski Petrovac, I would take that to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to now go to tab 193 in the presentation, this is master tab number 306, from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conclusions of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most, dated the 4th of June, 1992. Under item 1 of the conclusions: "Mirko Vrucinic, Nedeljko Rasula and Colonel Nedjo Anicic shall be in charge of resolving the issue of prisoners and their categorisation and deportation to Manjaca. 1st category - politicians; 2nd category - nationalist extremists; 3rd category - people unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any definition of that third category?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this document, no, of what is unwelcomed or undesired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take you next to tab 194 in the presentation, master tab 454.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report on some aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead, written by the Serbian Republic Ministry of the Interior, dated the 17th of July, 1992, and addressed to the president of the Presidency and the Prime Minister. That is added in handwriting on the front page, it's not in the letterhead that it's addressed. I'm just looking -- yes, it's on page 3 of the translation, and also the third page of the B/C/S, 03246858, in both cases the first paragraph. This is the Ministry of Interior reporting that: "The army, Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible, and they leave such undefined camps to internal affairs organs. The conditions in some of these camps are poor. There is no food. Individuals sometimes do not observe international norms ..." et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this was a report of which --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior, apparently to the president of the Presidency and to the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to show you presentation tab 195, master tab 295. This is a document we looked at earlier with a different excerpt, this one pertaining to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell us again what this report is.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the report of the police stations of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Bosanski Novi, as then compiled by the security services centre in Banja Luka. I had made a distinction in my report. Perhaps it's too fine a point to make a difference now, but in addition to establishing setting up detention centres and ordering the detention of various people or categories of people, Crisis Staffs also could order the transfer of prisoners between detention centres. So we see this on page 4 of the English, first sentence -- first paragraph, and it's on the bottom of the third page in the B/C/S, B0032529: "On 27 May 1992, pursuant to the decision of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor, all the prisoners from Keraterm facility in Prijedor were transferred to the facility in Omarska."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, I'd like to go to tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have a question, Witness. I would like to understand, what is the Commission for the Inspection of Municipalities? Could you please tell me what sort of organisation that is, what was its role? Were there several commissions in charge of inspections? Were there several commissions of that type? Who had set up these organisations? Can you please give us some background information about this institution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This appears to be a police institution rather than a municipal institution, and I don't know anything more about it than in this report, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we'll hear some evidence from some other witnesses about which institution established this commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding the timing of that report, the date on that report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: 18 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of anything that happened in connection with the detention facilities shortly prior to that time that may have had a relation to the creation of this commission?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They became publicly known at this time in the media. There was a great deal of international media attention on these detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition, I guess you've used these last two examples of prisoners being transferred in and out. Did you see some additional documentary evidence of that in the form of payment for transportation?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me refer you to tab 196, master tab 305, from Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the last page of the translation -- it's a series of documents, bills. We've seen some other bills from Zvornik before. If I can just -- yes, similarly, it's on the last page of the B/C/S, 01328458, a list of various transportations taken -- undertaken on the order of the provisional government by a transport company, and now they're charging the provisional government for it. The fourth item on the list, dated the 15th of July, 1992, "the transport of 600 prisoners from Zvornik via Bijeljina to Batkovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we've talked about the Crisis Staffs' involvement in deciding who gets put in detention facilities and the movement from detention facilities. Did you also see evidence that the Crisis Staffs were making decisions or issuing orders about who got released from detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a related power, they could also order the release.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you tab 197 in the presentation, master tab 460.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor from the 2nd of June, 1992. "Decision on the release of imprisoned persons. Article 1: All Serbs who have been imprisoned by mistake are hereby released from further imprisonment."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did it make any reference to non-Serbs imprisoned by mistake?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no reference to non-Serbs as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, I'd like to show you presentation tab 198. This is from Prijedor. It's master tab 278.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a document we've seen before, and perhaps it would have been more efficient to say everything at once, but I'd had, as I said, made some fine distinctions. The last -- on page 3 of the English, the third from the bottom, conclusion -- third paragraph from the bottom: "Conclusion of the 2nd of July, 1992, forbidding the individual release of prisoners from Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm." This was, again, the list of conclusions, orders, and decisions adopted by the Crisis Staff, the War Presidency of Prijedor relating to the SJB and the regional command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does this appear to be the order we saw referred to by the police as being followed by them?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I had said so at the time, but now I'm not sure about the date. If I could just check the date on that one, because I don't want to make a connection -- do you remember which tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm looking at the tab. I believe it's P184, or 183. These were both related to --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 183 is the same document, it's the list. My apologies. Yes, it can't be the same order, because it's a different number, and actually the report on the implementation predates by one day the date ascribed to this. So my apologies to my earlier assertion that we'd see that order. It's a similar order, apparently, but it is not the same order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go, then, to presentation tab 199, master tab 309. This is from Vogosca Crisis Staff, the 26th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another order of release, this by the Crisis Staff of Vogosca, the 26th of May, 1992. "The prison warden is ordered to release 154 people and take them to the village of Svrake, to Sarajevo and to Vogosca."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you presentation tab 200, master tab number 421. This is from the acting warden, Mr. Krnojelac, from Foca, on the 15th of May, 1992, addressed to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's forwarding to the Crisis Staff one detainee's request for release, indicating that he at least saw the Crisis Staff as having the authority to approve or not the request for release.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think that completes our examples concerning release of prisoners from detention centres -- detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next topic in your report, in paragraph 60 of your report, you talk about the status of non-Serbs in the Serb municipalities as being a theme of the work of the Crisis Staffs. And the first document I want to show you in connection with that is at presentation tab 201, master tab 310, from the Celinac municipality. Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision on the status of the non-Serb population of Celinac municipality, dated the 23rd of July, 1992, of the War Presidency of Celinac. It's fairly -- several pages, but it's an interesting Celinac. It's fairly -- several pages, but it's an interesting document, so I'll take you through some of it. First of all, the very title says what it's about, the status of the non-Serbs. And the War Presidency says in Article 1 that: "Combat operations in Celinac and elsewhere have given rise to basic reasons for giving the non-Serbian population of Celinac a special status." Article 2 is a listing of some of the non-Serbs, 34 names, mostly Muslim with one, apparently, Croat name, the last one. Article 3 says that citizens -- non-Serbs, because it says "citizens from Article 1," that means non-Serbs, "may live unhindered within the boundaries of their property to work and produce, to satisfy their day-to-day requirements." Article 4: "Non-Serbs shall be permitted to leave Celinac in an organised fashion, provided that the entire family household leaves." Under Article 5: "Non-Serbs are forbidden from moving around Celinac town between 1600 and 0600 hours. They are forbidden from lingering in the street, catering facilities, and other public places. They are forbidden from bathing in the rivers Vrbanja and Josava, hunting and fishing; forbidden from travelling from their settlement to other towns without permission from the competent municipal organ; forbidden from owning any kind of firearm, regardless of whether or not a permit to carry such has been issued; forbidden from moving or using cars; forbidden from gathering in groups with more than three men; forbidden from contacting relations who are not in the municipality; forbidden from using communications systems apart from the post office telephone; forbidden from wearing any kind of uniform; forbidden from selling real estate and exchanging apartments without special permission from the competent municipal organ." Article 6, they are obliged to show -- turn out for work obligations and not to do anything to desecrate the struggle of the Serbian people for its freedom. And then Article 7 is special restrictions on the people listed in Article 2. They may not make any contact with other people in the neighbourhood or further afield, and may not move between 0000 hours and 24 hours, essentially 24 hours a day, except when called for work obligation. Article 8, the War Presidency can offer -- can issue special consent that these do not apply to certain people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any information concerning the 1991 census data on the population of Celinac -- Celinac municipality?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. About 11 per cent of the population was Muslim, and the rest Serb. Virtually no Croats, as the list would suggest. And about 2.100 Muslims in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like, then, to show you presentation tab 202, which is master tab number 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one question: So do I well understand that these specific measures would apply to approximately 1 per cent, a little bit over 1 per cent, of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 11 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 11 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I'm looking at the list, the list in Article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 2, that specific measures, or would you say Article 1 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 1 is the non-Serb population. Then Article 2, they list certain people. And under Article 7, it is a little confusing, but under Article 7, they say those people named in Article 2, that is the list of people, they cannot move anywhere --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I missed the reference to -- yes, it's clear to me now. Thank you very much for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, do you have the next tab from Sipovo in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That document from Celinac is, by far, the most sweeping action of Crisis Staff or War Presidency on the status of non-Serbs, but we do see that, as I mentioned, as a theme in many Crisis Staffs' work. So on a smaller scale, but just to show that it was not the -- the preoccupation was not limited to Celinac, we have the minutes of the Sipovo municipal Crisis Staff, this one from the 19th of May, 1992. On page 5 in the translation, and in the B/C/S -- it will take me a moment, I apologise, to find. Because they are handwritten, it does take a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it's 02194138.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I have the right excerpt.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it looks right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we just say on the transcript that it's tab 202. Mr. Hannis referred to it as the next tab. It's quite a way back, just so that people reading it future can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. That's correct and it's master tab 119. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, it's on the top of the page you gave, 02194138, and on page 5 in the English, in the centre of the page, number 5. The Crisis Staff is discussing the distribution of humanitarian aid. One Crisis Staff notes that there are Muslims on the list of those supposed to receive social welfare, and another Crisis Staff member says that it should be discussed -- distributed exclusively to Serbs. The conclusion at this point is to refer that to the party. The Crisis Staff doesn't actually decide on that matter, but it's something of interest to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have another excerpt in this document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to refer to it when we get to the dismissals from employment. But if it's easier now --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Since we're close to ending time, why don't you talk about it now when you have the document out?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next page in the English, the bottom of page 6 in the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it's on 4139 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the bottom of that page in the B/C/S. "Firing Muslims from specific positions: In the post office; the fire station; the petrol station. Replace the butcher, and other Muslims in various management positions in Vitorog." Vitorog would be a company. I don't know of what.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I note the time. This would be a good time to end now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Just for our information, the Chamber is fully aware that we have caused a delay of one hour this morning. Is your time scheduling one hour more than you said yesterday, or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It might be slightly more. I looked at what remained last night. The case studies that we want to do for the three municipalities, I thought, would go quicker than this does, but at looking at the documents, it might go at the same rate or a little longer. I'm still hoping that maybe by eliminating some things I can finish by the end of the day tomorrow. I don't think I'll be done any earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Will you please take care that we can finish by tomorrow. Of course, you sometimes have to set some priorities, and it might be because, of course, some of the material here now is already in the footnotes, although we don't have the related documents, and sometimes it's just one line read from a document where -- well, we could have read that line from a document as well. So you're invited to do it in a way which draws our specific attention to the most important aspects you'd like to draw our attention to, and at the same time, you're instructed to finish your examination-in-chief by tomorrow. Ms. Hanson, with the amendment I gave in this hearing for your request, you're instructed not to speak with your colleagues, apart from the topic we discussed earlier, and I would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, in the same courtroom. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning.
